gems.title: ruaḥ — One Word for Three Realities
gems.insight: The Hebrew word רוּחַ means simultaneously 'spirit,' 'wind,' and 'breath' — there is no clean separation in Hebrew thought. When Genesis 1:2 says 'the רוּחַ of God hovered over the waters,' the original audience heard all three meanings layered together: the divine Spirit, the wind, the very breath of God. English forces a choice; Hebrew refuses it. Translators must pick one and lose the others.
gems.verseTranslation: And the Spirit/Wind/Breath of God hovered over the face of the waters.

gems.title: ḥesed — The Untranslatable Word
gems.insight: חֶסֶד is famously hard to render in English. It combines loyalty, kindness, faithfulness, and covenant love into one concept. KJV used 'lovingkindness' (a coined compound), modern versions use 'steadfast love' or 'covenant love.' It is what God shows to His covenant people — love that does not let go because of a sworn relationship. Used 248x in the OT, especially in the Psalms and the book of Ruth.
gems.verse: חַסְדֵי יְהוָה כִּי לֹא־תָמְנוּ כִּי לֹא־כָלוּ רַחֲמָיו
gems.verseTranslation: The steadfast loves of the LORD never cease; his mercies never come to an end.

gems.title: shalom — Peace Is Wholeness
gems.insight: שָׁלוֹם is far broader than English 'peace' (= absence of conflict). Its root שׁלם means 'whole, complete, intact.' Shalom is the state of nothing-missing, nothing-broken — comprehensive flourishing. When Israel greets with shalom, they pray for total well-being. When God promises shalom, He promises restored creation, not merely a ceasefire.
gems.verse: יִשָּׂא יְהוָה פָּנָיו אֵלֶיךָ וְיָשֵׂם לְךָ שָׁלוֹם
gems.verseTranslation: The LORD lift up his face to you and grant you peace [shalom].

gems.title: yada' — Knowing as Intimacy
gems.insight: Hebrew יָדַע means more than English 'know' (= mental cognition). It implies experiential, relational, even covenantal knowing. The same verb is used for Adam 'knowing' Eve sexually (Gen 4:1), for God 'knowing' Israel as His chosen people (Amos 3:2), and for prophetic knowing (Jer 1:5). To 'know' biblically is to be in relationship with — not just to have information about.
gems.verseTranslation: Before I formed you in the womb I knew you.

gems.title: nefesh — The Whole Living Being
gems.insight: נֶפֶשׁ is often translated 'soul,' but Hebrew has no body/soul dualism like Greek. נֶפֶשׁ is the WHOLE living being — sometimes translated 'life' (Lev 17:11: 'the life of the flesh is in the blood'), 'self' ('my נֶפֶשׁ longs for God' = 'I long'), or even 'throat' (the source of breath). Genesis 2:7 says man BECAME a נֶפֶשׁ — he didn't merely receive one. You don't have a nefesh; you ARE a nefesh.
gems.verse: וַיִּפַּח בְּאַפָּיו נִשְׁמַת חַיִּים וַיְהִי הָאָדָם לְנֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה
gems.verseTranslation: And he breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living being [nefesh].

gems.title: təhom — The Deep of Genesis 1
gems.insight: תְּהוֹם appears in Gen 1:2 ('darkness over the face of the deep') and is cognate with Akkadian Tiamat — the chaos-monster of the Babylonian creation epic. But notice what Genesis does: there is no battle, no struggle. God simply speaks; the deep submits. Genesis demythologizes the surrounding ANE worldview — what other cultures called a goddess Israel calls inert water under God's sovereign word.
gems.verseTranslation: And darkness was over the face of the deep.

gems.englishGloss: God, gods (plural form, often singular meaning)
gems.title: ʾElohim — Plural Form, Singular God
gems.insight: אֱלֹהִים is grammatically plural (-im ending) but takes a SINGULAR verb when referring to the God of Israel (Gen 1:1: 'אֱלֹהִים בָּרָא' — 'God [pl] CREATED [sg]'). The plural is often called the 'plural of majesty' or 'plural of intensity.' The same word can mean 'gods' (true plural) when referring to pagan deities — context determines. Classical Christian theology has long noted this grammatical hint at trinitarian fullness within divine unity.
gems.verse: בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים אֵת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְאֵת הָאָרֶץ
gems.verseTranslation: In the beginning God [pl] created [sg] the heavens and the earth.

gems.title: The Tetragrammaton
gems.insight: יְהוָה (the four-letter Name, YHWH) is the personal name of Israel's God, revealed at the burning bush (Ex 3:14) and connected to the verb הָיָה ('to be'). Out of reverence, Jews have not pronounced it for over 2,000 years — substituting אֲדֹנָי ('my Lord') when reading aloud. The Masoretes added the vowels of אֲדֹנָי to the consonants of יהוה, producing the hybrid 'Jehovah' (a misreading). Most English translations follow the substitution: rendered as the small-cap 'LORD' (vs. the title 'Lord' for אֲדֹנָי).
gems.verseTranslation: I AM WHO I AM.

gems.englishGloss: to create (only God is the subject)
gems.title: barāʾ — A Verb Only God Performs
gems.insight: בָּרָא ('create') is used with God as the subject 48 times in the OT — and ONLY with God. Humans never בָּרָא; they only עָשָׂה ('make') or יָצַר ('form'). The verb is reserved for the kind of bringing-into-existence that only the Creator can do. In Genesis 1, בָּרָא frames the entire chapter (1:1, 1:21, 1:27) — appearing at three creation milestones: cosmos, life, humanity.
gems.verseTranslation: In the beginning God created...

gems.title: bərit — Covenant Cuts the World in Two
gems.insight: בְּרִית (covenant) was 'cut' (כָּרַת בְּרִית) — never 'made.' The idiom comes from the ancient ritual of cutting animals in half and walking between the pieces (Gen 15:10-17), invoking the curse 'may I become like these animals if I break this covenant.' The Hebrew Bible structures itself around covenants: Noahic, Abrahamic, Mosaic, Davidic, New. Every Christian use of 'New Testament' (= 'New Covenant') traces to בְּרִית.
gems.verseTranslation: The LORD cut a covenant with Abram.

gems.englishGloss: heart (the seat of will and intellect, not emotion)
gems.title: lev — The Hebrew 'Heart' Is Your Mind
gems.insight: Hebrew לֵב refers to the seat of WILL, INTELLECT, and DECISION-MAKING — NOT emotion (modern English usage). When Deuteronomy 6:5 commands 'love the LORD with all your לֵב,' it means your COMMITMENT and THINKING, not your feelings. Emotion in Hebrew lives in the kidneys (כְּלָיוֹת), guts (מֵעִים), or bowels (רַחֲמִים — also the word for compassion). Re-reading the Bible with this in mind reframes what 'heart' verses ask of the reader.
gems.verse: מִכָּל־מִשְׁמָר נְצֹר לִבֶּךָ כִּי־מִמֶּנּוּ תּוֹצְאוֹת חַיִּים
gems.verseTranslation: Above all else, guard your heart [= guard your decisions/will], for from it flow the issues of life.

gems.title: təshuvah — Repentance as Returning
gems.insight: Hebrew has no word that exactly maps to English 'repent.' תְּשׁוּבָה is built on the root שׁוב ('to turn, return, come back'). To repent is not primarily to feel sorry — it is to TURN AROUND, to come back home. The prophets call Israel to שׁוּבוּ ('return!') over and over. In Jewish thought, the High Holy Days are a season of teshuvah — the soul's homecoming.
gems.verseTranslation: Return, O Israel, to the LORD your God.

gems.englishGloss: to confirm, to be firm; to believe (hifil)
gems.title: ʾaman — The Root of 'Amen' and 'Faith'
gems.insight: The root אמן conveys FIRMNESS, STABILITY, RELIABILITY. From it come: אָמֵן ('amen' = 'so let it be firm'), אֱמוּנָה ('faithfulness, faith'), הֶאֱמִין ('to believe' = to consider firm/reliable). When Genesis 15:6 says Abraham 'believed' (הֶאֱמִין) the LORD, it means he treated God's promise as solid bedrock. Faith in Hebrew thought is not 'wishful thinking' — it is leaning your whole weight on what is firm.
gems.verseTranslation: And he believed [treated as firm/reliable] in the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness.

gems.title: tsədaqah — Righteousness Is Relational
gems.insight: צְדָקָה means 'righteousness' but it is RELATIONAL, not an abstract moral standard. To be tzaddik (righteous) is to fulfill the demands of the relationship you stand in — to a covenant partner, to a king, to God. By Second Temple period, tzedakah had also come to mean ALMSGIVING (still its primary meaning in Modern Hebrew). The Hebrew imagination doesn't separate 'righteousness' from 'justice' — they are one word, one concept.
gems.verseTranslation: And he counted it to him as righteousness.

gems.title: shamaʿ — To Hear Is to Obey
gems.insight: In Hebrew, hearing and obeying are the SAME WORD. שָׁמַע means both 'hear' and 'obey' — distinguishing them requires context. When Moses cries 'שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל' (Deut 6:4, the Shema), he is not requesting auditory attention but COVENANT FIDELITY. To truly hear God is to obey God; to fail to obey is to have not really heard. Compare 1 Sam 15:22: 'to obey [שְׁמֹעַ] is better than sacrifice.'
gems.verse: שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ יְהוָה אֶחָד
gems.verseTranslation: Hear [obey], O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one.

gems.title: kavod — Glory Has Weight
gems.insight: כָּבוֹד ('glory') comes from the root כבד meaning 'heavy.' To 'glorify' someone in Hebrew is to give them WEIGHT, gravitas, substance. God's glory is His weighty, substantial Presence — that which fills the tabernacle so densely that Moses cannot enter (Ex 40:35). When NT Greek translates kavod as δόξα ('glory, opinion'), some of the sense of mass and substance is lost. Hebrew 'glory' is a thing you can feel pressing down on you.
gems.verse: וַיְכַס הֶעָנָן אֶת־אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד וּכְבוֹד יְהוָה מָלֵא אֶת־הַמִּשְׁכָּן
gems.verseTranslation: The cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory [weight] of the LORD filled the tabernacle.

gems.title: Three Words for Sin
gems.insight: Hebrew distinguishes three categories of sin: פֶּשַׁע ('transgression' — willful rebellion against authority), חַטָּאת ('sin' — missing the mark, falling short), עָוֹן ('iniquity' — twistedness, perversion). They appear together in confessional texts (Ex 34:7, Ps 32:1-5) to cover the full spectrum of moral failure. Modern English flattens them. Reading carefully: which Hebrew word stands behind 'sin' in any verse changes the nuance significantly.
gems.verseTranslation: Blessed is the one whose transgression [peshaʿ] is forgiven, whose sin [ḥaṭṭaʾt] is covered.

gems.title: ʾahav — Love as Covenant Loyalty
gems.insight: Hebrew אָהַב includes feeling but is primarily ACTION and LOYALTY. When God commands 'love your neighbor' (Lev 19:18), He is not commanding an emotion (you can't will an emotion) but a pattern of conduct. Same root used in ANE political treaties: a vassal king is required to 'love' the suzerain — meaning loyal service. So 'love the LORD with all your heart' (Deut 6:5) is COVENANT LANGUAGE, not romantic.
gems.verse: וְאָהַבְתָּ אֵת יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ בְּכָל־לְבָבְךָ וּבְכָל־נַפְשְׁךָ וּבְכָל־מְאֹדֶךָ
gems.verseTranslation: You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart, soul, and might.

gems.title: qadosh — Holy Means Set Apart
gems.insight: קָדוֹשׁ does not primarily mean 'morally pure' (modern English connotation). Its root meaning is SET APART, OTHER, distinct from common use. A holy vessel is one set apart for sacred use; the Sabbath is holy because it is set apart from other days. God is qadosh because He is utterly other, transcendent — wholly distinct from creation. Moral purity follows because what is set apart for God must reflect His character.
gems.verseTranslation: Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts.

gems.englishGloss: to walk; to live, to conduct one's life
gems.title: halakh — Walking Is Living
gems.insight: הָלַךְ literally means 'walk' but is used metaphorically for HOW ONE LIVES. To 'walk with God' (Enoch in Gen 5:24, Noah in Gen 6:9) means to conduct one's life in God's presence and direction. The post-biblical word HALAKHAH ('Jewish religious law') derives from this root: it is 'the way one walks.' This conceptual link runs through the NT as well (e.g., 'walk by the Spirit'), reflecting Hebrew background.
gems.verseTranslation: Enoch walked with God.

gems.title: ʿolam — From Distant Time to Cosmic Place
gems.insight: In biblical Hebrew, עוֹלָם means 'long duration' or 'far time' — both far past and far future, often translated 'forever' or 'eternal.' By post-biblical Hebrew, it had also taken on the spatial sense of 'world, universe' (its meaning in modern Hebrew). The shift from temporal to spatial happened because what is most permanent and distant is the cosmos itself. So 'God of עוֹלָם' meant 'God of distant time/eternity'; in later usage it implies 'God of the world.'
gems.verseTranslation: And he called there on the name of the LORD, the everlasting God [El Olam].

gems.title: panim — Why 'Face' Is Plural
gems.insight: פָּנִים ('face') is always grammatically PLURAL in Hebrew (-im ending), even when referring to one person's face. Theories: (1) the face has many features/expressions; (2) two-sided like a mountain has two slopes. Idioms: 'to seek God's face' = to seek His presence; 'God's face shines on you' = His favor; 'face to face' = direct encounter. The Aaronic blessing (Num 6:24-26) uses 'face' twice, asking that the LORD's face would shine and lift up upon you.
gems.verse: יָאֵר יְהוָה פָּנָיו אֵלֶיךָ וִיחֻנֶּךָּ יִשָּׂא יְהוָה פָּנָיו אֵלֶיךָ וְיָשֵׂם לְךָ שָׁלוֹם
gems.verseTranslation: The LORD make his face shine upon you and be gracious to you; the LORD lift up his face upon you and grant you peace.

gems.title: ʾemet — Truth as Reliability
gems.insight: Hebrew אֱמֶת ('truth') derives from the same root as אָמַן ('to be firm, reliable') — same root as 'amen.' So truth in Hebrew is not primarily 'correspondence to facts' (Greek/Western philosophical sense) but RELIABILITY, TRUSTWORTHINESS, FAITHFULNESS. God is אֱמֶת because He keeps His word, not merely because His statements are factually accurate. This is why חֶסֶד וֶאֱמֶת ('steadfast love and truth/faithfulness') often appears as a hendiadys for God's covenant character.
gems.verse: יְהוָה אֵל רַחוּם וְחַנּוּן אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם וְרַב־חֶסֶד וֶאֱמֶת
gems.verseTranslation: The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abundant in steadfast love and faithfulness.

gems.title: mishpaṭ — Justice as Right Ordering
gems.insight: מִשְׁפָּט covers a wider range than English 'justice.' It can mean: (1) a judicial verdict, (2) a legal ordinance/statute, (3) the right way of doing something (the 'mishpat' of building the temple = the proper procedure), (4) social/distributive justice. When Amos cries 'let justice [mishpat] roll down like waters' (5:24), he means right ordering of society — courts that work, the poor protected, the powerful held accountable.
gems.verse: וְיִגַּל כַּמַּיִם מִשְׁפָּט וּצְדָקָה כְּנַחַל אֵיתָן
gems.verseTranslation: Let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.

gems.title: torah — Not Just 'Law'
gems.insight: תּוֹרָה is conventionally translated 'law,' but its root יָרָה means 'to throw, to shoot' (an arrow), and metaphorically 'to point, to instruct.' תּוֹרָה is INSTRUCTION — what a parent teaches a child, what God teaches Israel. The legal-code sense is one specific application. When Psalm 1 calls the תּוֹרָה of the LORD a person's delight, it means the WHOLE FORMATIVE TEACHING of God, not merely His statutes. 'Torah' as a title for the Pentateuch reflects this broader sense.
gems.verse: כִּי אִם בְּתוֹרַת יְהוָה חֶפְצוֹ וּבְתוֹרָתוֹ יֶהְגֶּה יוֹמָם וָלָיְלָה
gems.verseTranslation: But his delight is in the law [instruction] of the LORD, and on his law he meditates day and night.
